BharatGen

We are from the Vision team at BharatGen. Patram is our vision-language model for Indian documents. This talk is about the system that generated its training data: Patram-Ingest, and specifically the layer around vLLM that decides whether the GPUs stay busy and whether a crash costs us any work.

Three numbers. 50.8 million training examples and 41.3 billion tokens were produced by this system. And in controlled fault-injection experiments, 198 injected failures of processes, nodes and model servers, plus three database failovers, lost and duplicated no record. The thesis of the talk is that durable execution is what makes this possible, and that it can be done cheaply.

Structure: first, how one node keeps GPUs busy, from first principles. Second, durable execution. Third, StageWeaver, the DAG layer. Fourth, the system around vLLM and how it evolved. Fifth, evaluation against existing frameworks.

What we build

Vision foundation models for Indian documents

One model reads the page image directly. No OCR first, so layout, tables and stamps are not lost on the way.
Many scripts on one page
Dense, tilted tables
Stamps and signatures

BharatGen builds foundation models for India. The Vision team builds vision-language foundation models, tools and applications for Indian documents. The model takes the page image as input. It does not run OCR first and pass text to a language model, because that loses layout, tables and stamps.

Indian documents are hard in specific ways: several scripts on one page, dense and slightly tilted tables, stamps and signatures, and faded scans or phone photos.

Where we are: e-VikrAI in 2024 generated product listings from a photo in Indian languages, and was named among IndiaAI's six notable Indian AI models of 2024. Patram-7B followed in June 2025, India's first sovereign vision-language model, released openly.

Then an ecosystem: task models such as grounding, layout and OCR, and agents for parsing, retrieval and translation, in use with partner organisations. Patram 1.5 is one model for 34 tasks, with promptable OCR and the ability to say "I don't know".

Next is Patram 2.0: all tasks and more than 22 Indian languages in one model. Each release needs more data and more infrastructure, which is what the rest of the talk is about.

Each system’s output is the next one’s input. We start at data generation.

Behind a model like Patram 1.5 are four systems, in the order the data moves.

Patram-Ingest makes the training data: models write the examples. More than 50 million examples for Patram 1.5. This is the subject of the talk.

Patram-FS stores and serves it: 68.7 terabytes of page images packed into 6,804 shards so training reads them at local-disk speed.

Patram-Core trains the model on 74 data sources across 192 GPUs.

PatramBench evaluates it on Indian documents: 17 domains and 150 document types. Each system's output is the next one's input. We start where the data starts, at generation.

The workload

One page becomes a chain of model calls

A teacher model reads a page and writes a training example. Each call needs the output of the one before.
input page
1

what is on the page

electricity bill, 4 tables
2

“What is the payment due date?”
3

Answer

“15 July 2015”

matches the page
time on the GPUsEach call waits for the previous one. Nothing here can run in parallel.
A formUnderstand›Extract fields›Verify
A blank pageUnderstand›dropped

The route depends on what the page contains.

Start with what we actually make. A modern document model is trained mostly on data written by other models. Take one scanned page, here an electricity bill. A teacher model first works out what is on the page. A second call writes a question about it. A third answers the question from the page. A fourth checks the answer against the page. That is one training example.

Watch the page go through. Each call takes seconds on a GPU, and each needs the output of the one before it.

So within one page nothing runs in parallel. The only way to keep GPUs busy is to have many pages in flight at once, which is the first problem of this talk.

And the route is not fixed. A form takes a different path from a table, and a blank page goes nowhere. We will come back to this when we reach graphs; for now keep the simple chain in mind as the running example.

At production scale

Millions of pages, dozens of nodes, days of runtime

0Mtraining examples generated for Patram 1.5
0Btokens of model output
0nodes in one run, 8 H100 GPUs each
daysfor a single pipeline run
About 390 GPUs to keep busy. Any of them can fail.

The numbers from our production runs for Patram 1.5: more than 50 million training examples, 41 billion tokens of model output, and up to 49 nodes in a single run, eight H100 GPUs each. A run takes days.

That is about 390 GPUs. They are expensive, so we want them busy. And at this scale something is always failing. The next slide is what that looked like.

What happens at this scale

A shared cluster where any process can fail

70.7 hto the first usable record when each stage was launched by hand, one at a time
9 of 24nodes stopped working in one run. Nobody noticed for six hours.
Servers are put to sleep, nodes are reclaimed, processes are killed, database primaries fail over.

The cluster is a pool of 50 H100 nodes with eight GPUs each, node-local NVMe, a shared parallel filesystem and an object store. There is no dedicated service node, and users may not install software on the nodes or run long-lived control services. A managed PostgreSQL cluster is the one shared service every node can reach. vLLM servers are hosted by a separate fleet layer that starts a server on every node whose GPUs are free, restarts crashes, and publishes the set of serving instances in a registry. Any pipeline may use any server, and an engineer who needs GPUs puts a few nodes' servers to sleep rather than killing a run.

We first ran pipelines the way most groups do: one stage at a time, each a batch-inference job launched by a person when the previous one drained. In one run of a three-stage pipeline the first usable record appeared after 70.7 hours, because answers could not start until every question was written. This is our stage-by-stage baseline.

Meanwhile the cluster lent and took back nodes. In another run, nine of 24 nodes stopped working and nobody noticed for six hours: there was nothing to notice with.

A pipeline over a hundred million samples meets every one of these many times, and must neither lose a record, write one twice, nor record an outage as a bad sample.

The obvious approach

Stage by stage delivers nothing until the end

Stage by stage

Each stage is launched when the previous one drains

Concurrent stages

All stages run at once, on shared model servers

0%usable records so far
0manual launches
Stop the run at 0%
Measured: first 1,000 usable records after 10.7 min vs 81 min (7.6×)total time 1.72 h vs 1.79 h
Simulation; same work, same hardware. Measured values: 16 emulated nodes, 10⁵ pages, paper §7.5.

The obvious way to run a multi-stage pipeline is one stage at a time: run stage one over everything, wait, check it, launch stage two. It is simple, and it is how most groups start. We did too.

Both runs here do the same work on the same hardware and finish together. The left run produces no usable record until the last stage starts, needs a person to launch each stage, and if you stop it halfway you hold half-processed data. The right run hands samples to the next stage as soon as a small group is committed, so finished records appear from the first minutes.

Stopping both at 45 percent: the stage-by-stage run has nothing to train on, the concurrent run already has a third of its records.

The measured version: with a four-stage pipeline over 10 to the 5 pages on 16 emulated nodes, the concurrent run produced its first thousand usable records after 10.7 minutes; the stage-by-stage run, where a script starts each layer the moment the previous one drains, after 81 minutes, 7.6 times later. And the concurrent run finished 4 percent sooner. So the work has to flow: every stage running at once, each sample moving on as soon as it is ready, on shared model servers. That asks a lot of the system, and we turn to it as three needs.

What the system must do

Three needs, and one catch

1

Busy GPUs

The GPUs are the expensive part. They should never wait for the host.

2

No lost work

Any process can die. Every record is still written exactly once.

3

Flexible graphs

Stages branch and merge on what the data contains.

The catch

Durable execution usually writes to the database at every step. Existing engines make 18 to 110 commits per page. We aim for 0.2.

From these two problems, three needs. We will take them in order.

First, busy GPUs. The GPUs are the expensive part of the cluster, and most of the engineering in the first half of this talk is about never letting them wait for the host.

Second, no lost work. Any process can die at any instant, and when the dust settles the output must hold every record exactly once, without a person cleaning up.

Third, flexible graphs. Stages should branch and merge based on what the data contains, with all stages running at once.

The catch is that the second need is normally expensive. Durable execution engines record every step in a database. In our measurements, DBOS made 18 commits per page and Temporal 42 to 110,. We made 0.2. The next two parts are how: first busy GPUs, then durability.

Principle

GPU utilization is decided by the host

prepare: prompts, image checks GPU inference finish: parse, validate, write, fsync, commit idle
Host work is not removed. It is hidden behind GPU time.

Start from what a GPU is waiting for. For every batch the host has work to do: build prompts, check and read images, parse and validate the outputs, write results and fsync them, and update the database. The GPU does one thing: inference. Whether the GPU is busy depends entirely on how the host schedules that work around it.

The simplest structure is serial: prepare, call, wait for the answer, finish, repeat. The call blocks the host, and while the host finishes the previous batch the GPU has nothing to do. With one unit of preparation, three of inference and one of finishing, the GPU is busy 60 percent of the time, and the only way to improve it is to make the host faster.

The overlapped structure keeps three activities in flight at once: the GPU runs batch k, the host prepares batch k plus one and finishes batch k minus one. The same host work is still done, but none of it is on the GPU's critical path. After the first batch fills the pipeline the GPU is never waiting.

So the design question is not how to make the host work faster; it is how to arrange that the host is always one batch ahead. The next slides take that apart: what blocks, how many calls must be open, and how a node is structured to stay ahead.

First principles

Blocking and non-blocking calls

Blocking

The caller is suspended until the result is ready.

1 thread per call in flight

Non-blocking

The call returns at once. Completion is signalled later.

1 thread holds all calls in flight

async / await

Non-blocking code written as straight-line code.

async def call(req): r = await client.post(url, req) return validate(r) out = await gather(*(call(r) for r in batch))
the runtime resumes each call when its reply arrives
Waiting costs no CPU. A blocked thread still costs a stack and a scheduler slot. An event loop holds thousands of waits on one thread.

The vocabulary first, because everything later depends on it. A call to a model server spends almost all of its time waiting: the request is queued and generated on the server, and the client does nothing.

A blocking call suspends the caller until the result is ready. To keep many calls in flight with blocking calls you need one thread per call. Each thread is mostly waiting, so it uses almost no CPU, but it still costs a stack and a scheduler slot, and the thread count has to grow with the number of in-flight requests.

A non-blocking call returns immediately and completion is signalled later, through a callback or an event. One thread can then register thousands of pending calls with the operating system and be woken only when a reply arrives. That is an event loop.

async and await are the way to write that without callbacks: the function reads like straight-line code, and the runtime suspends it at each await and resumes it when the reply arrives. In our worker pool, which loop to use is decided by one fact: if the call function is a coroutine, the worker runs an event loop holding up to max-in-flight calls; otherwise it uses a simple get-one, answer-one loop. A vLLM client is the first kind; a headless browser is the second.

First principles

How many calls must be in flight

Little’s law
L = λ · W
L calls in flight
λ throughput
W latency per call

W ≈ 25 s per request

1 server admits 24 at once → λ = 24 / 25 = 0.96 /s

1 node = 4 servers → L = 96 in flight, λ ≈ 3.8 /s

Throughput of one node

requests per second against the number of calls the client keeps in flight

How many calls must the client keep open? Little's law answers it from first principles: the number of items in a system equals throughput times latency.

Our teacher model's mean latency is about 25 seconds per request. A server admits 24 requests at once, like any continuously batching engine, so one server completes 24 over 25, about 0.96 requests per second. A production node has four servers. To keep all four saturated the client must hold 4 times 24, which is 96, calls in flight. At that point a node completes about 3.8 requests per second, which matches the 3.88 we measure on one node.

The curve is the consequence. Below 96 in flight the servers are under-fed: throughput rises linearly with the window because the GPU has spare capacity, and every unused slot is idle hardware. Above 96 more calls only add queueing time without adding throughput.

So the client must sustain a window of about a hundred open calls per node, continuously. That is the requirement that dictates the call path: it cannot be a thread per call, and it cannot be batch-then-wait. It must be non-blocking, and it must be fed by a producer that is always ahead of it.

Design

Staying ahead of the GPU

rows held ≤ capacity + 2 × batch + commit group 0 when no server is serving

This is the structure of one stage on one node. Work flows left to right: claim rows from the database, prepare requests on a prep thread, submit them to the worker pool, which holds up to the capacity of all servers in flight, collect and validate responses on a collector thread as they stream back, and hand them to a writer thread that appends, fsyncs and commits in groups.

The key property is that every stage has its own thread and its own bounded buffer, so each one can proceed while the others are busy. Submission runs on its own thread, so the GPU is fed independently of how long the main loop spends fetching, writing or fsyncing. Results stream per request, so there is no batch boundary for a slow request to stall.

The number of rows a stage holds is controlled by conservation, not by timing. It holds the pool's live capacity plus two batches, one being prepared and one being committed, plus the commit group being written. Too little and the GPU starves; too much and one node hoards rows that another node could process.

And when nothing can serve, because every server this node uses is asleep, the stage holds zero rows. Work is therefore never parked on a node that cannot do it.

Design

Processes, threads and event loops

Processes

Separate GIL for CPU-bound work. Separate failure domain. One CUDA context per GPU.

Threads

Waits that release the GIL: database, fsync, uploads. Cheap hand-off through queues.

Event loops

Many calls in flight per worker, without a thread per call.

Private inboxes

No lock is shared across a process that can be killed.

This is how the node is built, and the reason for each choice. Three kinds of concurrency, each used where it fits.

Processes. Everything that is CPU-bound or that can fail independently runs in its own process: each stage worker, each model worker, the sweep, and the group leader that owns the shared backend. Python threads share one GIL, so CPU-bound work such as image checks, rendering or JSON handling would contend; separate processes do not. A process is also a failure domain: an out-of-memory kill or a SIGKILL takes down one process and nothing else shares its memory. And a GPU is owned by one process with its own CUDA context. Historically we ran the model service in the same process as the stage, and with up to ten stages' worth of Python in one process the GIL was the first bottleneck.

Threads. Inside a stage process, the work that is mostly waiting runs in threads: the prep thread, the collector thread, the writer thread that appends, fsyncs and commits, and the uploader that moves shards to the object store. Database round trips, fsync and network transfers release the GIL, so threads give real overlap, and hand-off through in-process queues is cheap. The writer is a single thread that owns the commit sequence, which keeps its ordering simple to reason about.

Event loops. Inside a model worker, an asyncio loop holds up to the worker's in-flight limit of calls, for example 24 per server. That is the non-blocking structure from the earlier slides: one thread, many waits. Workers whose call is synchronous, such as headless browsers, use a simple loop instead, one worker per browser.

Between processes we use queues, and here we learned a lesson: with one shared request queue, a worker killed while waiting on it holds the queue's reader lock forever and every surviving worker blocks. So there is now one dispatcher thread, the queue's only consumer, and a private inbox per worker; a killed worker can only poison its own. That is the next slide.

Failure case

A shared lock must not outlive its holder

Before: one shared request queue

pool: healthy, 4 / 4 workersthroughput 100%

After: dispatcher and private inboxes

pool: healthy, 4 / 4 workersthroughput 100%
3 / 8trials hung: kill 1 of 2 workers
→
0 hangsand 40 / 40 committed with 1 of 4 killed

A concrete multiprocessing failure, because it shaped the design. Through version 1.9.1 our worker pool was the simplest possible: one shared multiprocessing queue, N workers, all reading from it. A queue get holds the queue's internal reader lock while it waits. A process killed with SIGKILL runs no cleanup, so if it is the one holding the lock, the lock is held forever by a process that no longer exists.

The supervisor notices the dead worker and respawns it, and the pool reports healthy with the correct worker count. But every surviving worker is blocked on a lock that will never be released. Throughput is zero, with no error and no timeout.

The fix is not a safer lock; holding a lock across SIGKILL is a property of the primitive. The fix is to remove the shared lock from the hot path: one dispatcher thread is the shared queue's only consumer and hands each request to a private per-worker inbox. A killed worker can only poison its own inbox, which is discarded when the worker respawns.

Only one worker holds the lock at a time, so a kill hits it about one time in N. We measured rather than estimated: killing one of two workers mid-request, the old pool hung in 3 of 8 trials.

After the change: no hangs, and with one of four workers killed all 40 images committed with none failed. One limit remains and we state it: the response path still uses shared queues, so the same class of failure is possible in a much narrower window.

Backends

Five ways to run a model, and what each taught us

v1.0

batch

Batch generate() in the pipeline process

GIL, image copiesv1.5

async

Continuous batching: +29%

quality gap vs servev1.6

online

Local vllm serve over HTTP

one server per runv1.9.9

hosted

Shared servers; no GPUs on ingest nodes

any backendv1.9

function

Chrome, SAM3, YOLO, any model

The model backend changed five times, and each change was a response to something measured.

Version 1.0 ran the model's batch generate call inside the pipeline process. The whole batch waits for its slowest request, and with up to ten stages in one process they share one GIL. That led to the next three moves: a separate process, shared memory, and continuous batching.

Version 1.5 used vLLM's asynchronous engine with continuous batching, 29 percent faster. We then noticed outputs differed from, and were worse than, a normal vllm serve for the same model and the same engine arguments. Matching the arguments was not enough: the entry point that constructs the engine picks scheduler defaults, and the HTTP layer merges the model's generation config. The lesson was to run the model the way vLLM itself serves it.

Version 1.6 drives a local vllm serve subprocess over HTTP. The server renders prompts and reads the image files, so a request is just paths and text, and one wire contract serves every backend. That made our shared-memory work unnecessary. But each run still owned its server.

Version 1.9.9 added hosted servers: the fleet layer starts them, ingestion nodes need no GPUs, and many pipelines share them. That forced three new problems: discovering servers as they come and go, surviving sleep and wake, and judging health fairly under load.

In parallel, version 1.9 generalised the engine so that any Python function is a backend: headless Chrome rendering, SAM3, YOLO, a Hugging Face model. A backend is three functions: initialise, call and terminate. vLLM became one more worker specification, and the supervision code shrank to one worker pool.

The system around vLLM

Hosted vLLM as shared infrastructure

1

Ingest next to its servers

images are on that node’s NVMe

2

Same image, same server

reuse the vision cache: 1.5–1.9× prefill

3

Discover servers

a registry lists who is serving

4

Read records at the server

patram:// via the node’s daemon

vLLM provides a very good server. Operating it as shared infrastructure for a data pipeline needed four decisions around it.

One ingest process per node, pointed at that node's own servers. This is driven by data locality: images are read from the node's local NVMe instead of the shared filesystem, and a vLLM server cannot open another node's NVMe. Throughput then scales by adding nodes, all sharing one database.

Hash routing for workloads with several queries per image. If those queries spread across servers, each server re-encodes the same image. We hash the exact image path modulo the number of servers so all queries for an image reach the same server. With prefix caching and a multimodal processor cache that gave 100 percent vision KV-cache hits and a 1.5 to 1.9 times prefill speedup. The dots show the effect: with least-loaded routing the hit rate hovers around half; with hashing every server sees only its images. Hash routing is opt-in; least-loaded is the default.

The user names only the model. A registry lists the servers that are serving now, and the pool keeps one worker per serving server on this node, re-reading every 30 seconds. Previously URLs were typed in and the worker set was fixed, so a server woken later was never used.

The newest piece: a patram:// URI goes straight to vLLM. A plugin on the server reads the record through its node's storage daemon, so the client no longer writes every image to NVMe and deletes it afterwards. We validated that the model input is identical to the file path on 640 real records from 16 datasets and 25 decode edge cases.

Scaling and recovery

Pipelines follow shared servers

On a shared cluster the set of model servers a run can use changes under it all the time, so pipelines own no GPUs. The fleet layer hosts, restarts and lists servers; each pipeline follows them.

Every thirty seconds each pool re-reads the registry, spawns a worker for every new server and retires the worker of every server that has gone, handing its requests back without blame. A run can start before any server exists and begins the moment one appears.

When a server is put to sleep, its worker marks itself paused so the dispatcher sends it nothing, lets held requests finish for a sixty-second grace period, cancels the rest without blame, and probes the server with a backoff from five to thirty seconds. A paused pool holds no rows, so other nodes' servers take the work meanwhile.

When the server wakes and reappears in the registry, it answers again within seconds.

And since nobody owns a server, any number of pipelines from any team share the same hosted models. Liveness is read from progress, not probes: with work queued, a server is serving if its generated-token counter moves within fifteen seconds. An earlier version sent a one-token probe, which on a busy server waits in the queue too, and once left one of thirty nodes working.

The idea

Make coordination durable, and write it in bulk

Observation

A batch spends tens of seconds in model calls. Coordination is a few database writes.

ϕ = k·c / T= 3 × 5–25 ms / 20–30 s0.05 – 0.4 % of runtime
Two rules
Rule 1Every coordination write is idempotent
Rule 2No fact is recorded before it is true
Nothing that matters lives in a process. The command that starts a stage also recovers it.

We have three needs: busy GPUs, no lost work, flexible graphs. The first is a host problem and we have just solved it. For the second we need durable execution, and the usual price is a database write for every step. Our observation is that this workload can afford durable coordination if it is written in bulk.

A sample spends tens of seconds in model calls. A batch costs a constant number k of queries, claim, commit and hand-off, each taking time c, while the batch spends time T in the model. So coordination adds a fraction phi equals k c over T of the runtime, independent of batch size and of the number of nodes. With k of 3, c of 5 to 25 milliseconds and T of 20 to 30 seconds, that is 0.05 to 0.4 percent. And the records themselves need not enter the database at all.

Because a process can die between two writes, two rules. Every write is idempotent, so running it twice is the same as running it once. And a write that records a fact never precedes the write that makes the fact true. Everything in the rest of the talk is these two rules applied to a stage, to a graph, and to the model servers.

If every coordination action is such a write, nothing that matters lives in a process. The command that starts a stage is also the command that recovers it.

Durable execution

Two models of durable execution

Per-step durability

DBOS, Temporal: every step of every sample is a database transaction that stores the step’s output.

0transactions so far

Bulk durability Patram-Ingest

Records go to append-only shards. The database holds only coordination state, written per batch.

0transactions so far
18 · 42–110 → 0.2commits per page: DBOS · Temporal → Patram-Ingest
254–1,112 → 11–12KB of log per page
Same PostgreSQL, same emulated servers, 32 KB answers · paper §7.3

Durable-execution engines are the closest prior systems: a workflow per sample that routes by content, runs on any machine and recovers by itself. They make that possible by turning every step into a durable transaction.

In DBOS and Temporal every step of every sample is its own transaction that stores the step's output. That gives step-level recovery and also timers, signals and side-effecting steps. The cost is that the database carries tens of transactions per sample and every intermediate output, so with production-sized answers it becomes the bottleneck.

Our observation is that this workload doesn't need step-level durability, because a sample spends tens of seconds in model calls and redoing a step costs little. So we keep the records out of the database entirely: stage workers append them to shards on local disk. The database holds only coordination state, and it is written once per batch, not once per step.

Measured on the same database with the same emulated servers: about 0.2 commits per page against 18 for DBOS and 42 to 110 for Temporal, which is roughly 90 times fewer than DBOS and 200 to 600 times fewer than Temporal. The log written per page is 11 to 12 kilobytes against 254 to 1,112. We will return to what that buys at the end.

Stage worker · Algorithm 1

Commit order and crash points

After a crash here

Work redone
rule No fact is recorded before it is true

This is one stage worker's commit sequence, and the heart of the exactly-once guarantee. I'll kill the process at each step and say what recovery does. The rule is that a write that records a fact never precedes the write that makes the fact true.

A stage worker claims a batch of rows, builds requests, and as results arrive it appends each record to the shard. Every g records, the commit group, it fsyncs, then hands the samples to their next stages, then records the hand-off in the ledger, and only then marks the rows done with each record's shard address. The commit group is the replay bound: g is 250 on our shared parallel filesystem so fsyncs never leave the GPUs idle, and 16 is enough where the disk is fast.

Claimed: the row is processing and stamped with this node. On restart every such row is returned to the queue.

Requested: the request is in flight on a worker. If the worker dies, the pool answers its requests as infrastructure failures and respawns it; if the whole process dies, the rows are requeued as before.

Result in memory: it dies with the process and the sample is processed again. It is not marked failed, because the process dying says nothing about the sample.

Appended: the record is in the OS buffer, possibly torn. No row confirms it, so recovery truncates it and the sample is redone. At most one commit group is affected.

Fsynced: the record is durable, but no row says done. The database is the single source of truth, so this record is truncated too and redone. It looks wasteful but it means the files and the database can never disagree and nobody reconciles anything by hand.

Handed on: the downstream queue rows exist but the ledger's told bit is not yet set. The next sweep, or the restarted stage, repeats the queue write; it is guarded by pending state, so it changes nothing.

Told: the bit is set; the rows are still not done, so the stage redoes them and repeats the hand-off. OR-ing a bit twice changes nothing.

Marked done: committed, never replayed. Two invariants follow from the order. First, if a row is done then its record is on durable storage. Second, if bit t of a sample's told mask is set, the sample's row in stage t's queue is no longer pending.

So: after any sequence of crashes, if every crashed node restarts, every sample reaches every stage its route names, each stage's record appears in the committed index exactly once, and each crash redoes at most the g records of the group being written.

Architecture

State: one database, append-only shards

The design uses three kinds of durable state, and no process holds anything that matters.

Queue tables: every stage has a table with one row per sample of the corpus. A row's state is pending, processing, done, failed, upstream-ready or upstream-failed. It records the node working on it and, once done, the shard address of its record.

The ledger: one row per sample in flight, with two integers recording which stages have finished it and which have been handed it. I'll come back to this in the StageWeaver section. Three small control tables hold per-node row counts, node start and exit events, and stop requests.

Output shards: each stage worker appends records to a JSONL shard and image bytes to a tar shard on node-local disk. Shards rotate at a size bound and move to the object store in the background, and a record's shard address is what a later stage receives as its input.

The important property is that processes never talk to each other. They write to the database and to shards. There is no master, lease or heartbeat, and no operator. A node joins a run by starting the program and leaves by dying, and no table records the size of a run.

Stage worker

Claiming work from a table

queue table

one row per sample
pendingprocessingdone
UPDATE queue SET state='processing', node='B' WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM queue WHERE state='pending' LIMIT 64 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) RETURNING id;

Each stage needs many nodes working on it, so something has to decide who does what. If two nodes take the same sample we pay twice; if a sample falls between them it is never done. The usual answer is a coordinator process, which is one more thing the cluster can take away.

We use the database instead. A stage worker claims a batch with one statement: select up to b rows in its fetch state, lock them with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, set them to processing and stamp its node name, all in one transaction. Two workers claiming at the same instant skip each other's rows and neither waits. The SQL on the slide is a sketch of the pattern.

A node dies. Its rows are still processing and stamped with its name, and when it restarts they return to the queue. Until then no other node touches them, because the rows are locked by state, and if the node never returns a watcher on another node releases rows whose counters have not moved for ten minutes.

Nothing is assigned in advance, so a fast node takes more work than a slow one. To grow a run you start the same program on another node.

Recovery

Recovery is the start-up path

Shard on disk
Queue rows
1

Return every row processing and stamped with this node to its fetch state

2

Truncate the shard after the last record whose row is done and stamped with this node

No timeout, lease or heartbeat: a starting process holds nothing, so any row it stamped is abandoned by definition.

Recovery has no separate mode. The restarted program runs two steps before it fetches anything.

Here a stage was running. Its shard holds some records that rows confirm as done, and a trailing group that was appended but whose rows were never marked done, because the process died before that write.

Step one: one statement returns every row in state processing that is stamped with this node to its fetch state. A process that is starting holds nothing, so every such row is abandoned by definition, with no timeout, lease or heartbeat to evaluate.

Step two: it walks back from the last record of its newest shard to the last one whose row is done and stamped with this node, truncates everything after, and starts a fresh shard. Only trailing records are truncated, since byte offsets already handed to later stages must not move. Shards moving to the object store follow the same rule: the uploader copies a shard, repoints every row that names the old path with a compare-and-swap on the path this node wrote, then deletes the local file. Re-running the uploader at startup is the whole recovery.

There is no state a process has to remember, so the same command that starts a stage also recovers it. A node that never comes back is released by a watcher elsewhere. The guarantee: a crash redoes at most the rows it held and writes no record twice.

Cost model

Why one database is enough

Coordination fraction
ϕ = k·c / T
k queries per batch: claim, commit, hand-off
c time per query: 5–25 ms
T time in the model: 20–30 s

k = 3 → 0.05 – 0.4 % of runtime

independent of batch size and node count

measured gap to a bare client: 0.3 – 1.2 %

Database cost per page

32 KB answers, same PostgreSQL

Putting every coordination action through one database is affordable only because the work is slow. A batch of b samples costs a constant number k of queries, each taking time c, while the batch spends time T in the model. So coordination adds a fraction phi equals k c over T of the runtime, independent of b and of the number of nodes.

With k of 3, c of 5 to 25 milliseconds and T of 20 to 30 seconds, phi is 0.05 to 0.4 percent. Against a client with no coordination at all we measure a gap of 0.3 to 1.2 percent, which also covers the shard writes.

The other cost is load, because one database serves the whole run. A run finishing r samples per second through S stages issues r S k over b transactions per second, and the records go to shards, never into a table. An engine that makes each step of each sample durable issues at least r S transactions per second and stores every step's output with them. The ratio is at least b over k, about 20 with our batch of 64. Measured against DBOS it is 90.

The log tells the same story: 11 to 12 kilobytes per page against 254 to 283 for DBOS and 329 to 1,112 for Temporal, because we store coordination state, not outputs. The database itself is ordinary managed PostgreSQL with synchronous replication to one standby, so a failover loses no acknowledged commit, and every connection retries connection-class errors against a 30-second budget that outlasts a failover.

Why a line is not enough

Real pipelines are graphs

A page’s path depends on what earlier stages found.
1
Route by content charts, tables and forms go to different stages
 2
Start on any input a stage fires when one of its inputs is ready
 3
Stop early a blank page goes nowhere

So far the pipeline looked like a line: understand, ask, answer, verify. Real pipelines are not lines. Press the buttons, or run all pages, and watch where each page goes. Each stage is a model call with a prompt and a validator, a headless browser, or plain code.

The path depends on content. The understanding stage's routing function sends each page to one specialist: charts to the chart reader, forms to the field extractor, and a blank page nowhere. Questions starts as soon as any one of its inputs is ready; forms skip it. Two pages in the same batch take different routes. The grey numbers are the stage bit positions, which matter later.

Three things an engine must support: routing by content, starting a stage on any one of its inputs, and ending early. The rest of this act is how we do that with two bits of state per sample and no coordinator, once we have a way not to lose work.

StageWeaver · design questions · 1 of 2

The questions we had to answer first

Design questionConsideredDecisionConsequence
1Where does graph state live, so a crash cannot lose it?an in-memory coordinatorOne database row per sample in flight. The DAG itself is rebuilt from code at start-up.nothing to lose or elect
2How does a fan-in start exactly once when inputs finish on different machines, in any order?a fan-in tracker table per edgeTwo bitmasks per sample: done and told.one table instead of three
3How do content routing and fan-in coexist without special cases?topology-specific logicTwo activation paths that never reach the same stage, enforced at start-up.one code path for every topology
4What if a process dies between deciding to hand on and doing it?transactions across stage databasesQueue write first, told bit second, all idempotent. A sweep repairs gaps.no state correct in one place and wrong in another

When we started the DAG design in April, the engine could only run linear chains: stage N wrote a completion signal into stage N plus 1's database. That breaks down when the graph has branches, merges, conditional routing or several entry points, and it all had to be crash-safe and self-recovering. The design document opens with five goals: no new abstractions for stage authors, one code path for all topologies, the DAG in memory only, one flat table, and self-healing on crash. These are the questions that came up, and what we decided.

One: where does the state of the graph live? The conventional answer is a coordinator tracking every sample in memory, which the cluster can take away. We asked what it actually needs: which stages have finished a sample, and which have been told about it. That is a small amount of state per sample, so it goes into a database row. The graph's structure, the DAG, is not persisted at all: it is rebuilt from the stage declarations at start-up, because if the declarations change every stored mask is invalid anyway, and persisting the structure would create a versioning problem for no benefit.

Two: fan-in. The first design had a separate fan-in tracker with per-edge state and a lifecycle table. We collapsed it into the same two integers: a stage's required mask and a policy, all or any, turn the question into a bitwise test on one row, so one table does the job of three.

Three: routing and fan-in. A stage is entered either by explicit activation, a routing function naming it, or by a mask test, never both. If a routing target also declared upstreams it would be reachable through both paths and could be started twice, so the engine rejects that at start-up. Because the two never overlap they compose freely: a routed stage can fan out to stages that fan in from other branches, with no special cases.

Four: the crash window. Doing the hand-off and recording it cannot be one transaction because they touch different databases. So the order is the guarantee: the write that makes the hand-off true comes first, the bit that records it second, and both are idempotent. If a process dies between them, the bit is still clear and the sweep repeats the first write, which changes nothing.

StageWeaver · design questions · 2 of 2

The questions we had to answer first

Design questionConsideredDecisionConsequence
5How do stage authors stay unaware of the graph?stages that name their downstreamsStages declare upstreams only and make one completion call. Downstreams are inferred.no inconsistent edges
6How do stages share a model without sharing a process?stages as threads of one processA group leader owns the backend. One process per stage; shared request queue, private response queues.separate GIL and failure domain, one model copy
7Can a graph loop, for example verify and retry?structural cyclesAcyclic graphs. Bounded retries are expressed in routing functions.cycles rejected at start-up
8How large does coordination state grow?per-sample historyRows are deleted when every leaf is done.≈ 110 bytes per sample in flight

The second set of questions.

Five: how do stage authors stay unaware of the graph? Stages declare only their upstreams and make one completion call. Downstream relationships are inferred by the coordinator at start-up, which removes the possibility of inconsistent declarations, where A says it feeds B but B does not list A.

Six: the process model. The first version ran stages as threads inside one process per initialization group, sharing the loaded model. That kept one copy of the model but put every stage under one GIL and one failure domain. In May we rewired it: one process per stage, with a group-leader process per initialization source that owns the backend's lifecycle, spawns the stage processes and tears the backend down last. Stages in a group share one request queue into the pool and each gets a private response queue. Each stage process builds its own coordinator connection, because a database connection is not picklable.

Seven: loops. Verification loops are common, but a structural cycle makes completion undecidable for the leaf test. So the graph must be acyclic, and a retry is expressed as a bounded decision in a routing function, with a counter in the sample's output so it cannot loop forever.

Eight: size. The ledger holds one small row per sample in flight, about 110 bytes, and a row is deleted when every leaf is done or the sample can go no further, so it scales with work in progress, not with the corpus.

StageWeaver · the ledger

Two bitmasks per sample

ready (all)done ∧ R = R and told ∧ 2s = 0
ready (any)done ∧ R ≠ 0 and told ∧ 2s = 0
finisheddone ∧ L = L
One sample’s row through the pipeline of the workload slide · paper Figure 5

Each stage has a bit position, and each sample in flight has one row in the ledger holding two integers: done, the set of stages that have finished the sample, and told, the set of stages that have been handed it. The graph compiles at start-up into a few constant masks: a fan-in stage has an input mask R with one bit per input and a policy, all or any, and the leaves of the graph form a mask L. Every question a coordinator would have answered is then a bitwise test on one row.

Follow a chart page. It is seeded with the root's told bit set.

Understand finishes: done has bit 0. Its routing function says chart, so Charts is handed the sample and told gets bit 1.

Charts finishes: done has bits 0 and 1. Questions is a fan-in stage that waits for any of Charts, Tables and Text: done AND R-Questions is non-zero, and Questions is not yet told. The sweep hands the sample to Questions and sets its told bit.

Questions finishes. Verify waits for any of Forms and Questions, so now it is ready; the sweep tells it.

Verify finishes. Verify is the only leaf, so done AND L equals L, and the row is deleted. The ledger therefore holds one small row per sample in flight rather than per sample in the corpus. And because told records each activation, a fan-in stage starts exactly once even if a sweep is repeated or taken over by another node.

StageWeaver · activation paths

Fan-in is a query; routing is a write

Routing path

The stage that produced the content decides immediately.

Sweep path

One query per fan-in stage, every 5 s, over all samples in flight.

Routing: 250 samples handed on in 22 ms median, 47 ms p99
Sweep: a sample waits 2.3 s median, 5.1 s p99; a pass over 10⁶ samples in flight takes 663 ms
A stage is entered by one path only. The engine checks this, acyclicity and reachability at start-up.

The two questions after a stage finishes a sample are: where does it go next, and may a fan-in stage now start. They have different natures, so they get different paths.

Routing is a write. Where next is a decision about content, and the stage that just produced the content can make it immediately. When a stage finishes a batch it calls the author's routing function on the batch's outputs, receives for each sample the stages to send it to, groups the answer by target, and issues the same two writes, queue rows and told bits, one pair per target rather than per sample.

Fan-in is a query. Because the state is in the database, a fan-in condition need not be evaluated sample by sample. Every five seconds a sweep, for each fan-in stage, selects every sample whose row passes the stage's test and hands them all on together. It does not matter which machine finished the last input, because the sweep reads the durable result rather than listening for events. Every node tries to run the sweep but a database lock admits one at a time, because concurrent passes deadlock on the ledger, and the database frees the lock if its holder dies.

The two paths never reach the same stage: a stage with inputs is entered only by the sweep, and a routing target has an empty input mask, which keeps the sweep away. The engine checks this split, acyclicity and reachability at start-up, which is why one completion path serves content-based branches, fan-out, all and any fan-in, and routing into a later fan-in stage. Costs: a routing hand-off of 250 samples took 22 milliseconds median; a sample on the sweep path waits 2.3 seconds median, set by the five-second interval; and a sweep pass scans the ledger so its time grows with samples in flight, 13, 70 and 663 milliseconds at 10 to the 4, 5 and 6 samples.

StageWeaver · runtime

Process layout of a graph

The runtime is a tree of processes. The main process validates the graph, runs ingestion, and spawns one sweep process and one group-leader process per initialization source. Each group leader runs the group's init function, which starts the backend, spawns one process per stage in the group, joins them, and only then tears the backend down.

Each stage worker is its own process with its own database connection. Stages in the same group share one request queue into the pool and each has a private response queue, routed by stage name.

Models are therefore shared without sharing a process. A verifier stage can use the model server that an earlier stage already started instead of loading its own, while keeping its own GIL and failure domain.

Shutdown follows the same tree. The supervisors, the main process and each group leader, forward SIGTERM to their children and outlive them, because a group leader that unwound immediately would tear down the shared model while its stages were still using it. The resulting shutdown is the ordinary completion path, so a stage that is stopped early is indistinguishable from one whose work ran out: a two-stage graph with 16 rows in flight comes down in 7.5 seconds with no row stranded and no orphan process holding a GPU.

StageWeaver

What StageWeaver supports

A graph of stages declared in code. Coordination lives in the database, never in a process.
Arbitrary DAGschains, fan-out, fan-in
Routing functionseach sample picks its next stage
Fan-in policieswait for all inputs, or any
Several roots and sinksindependent entry points
Shared modelsstages in a group share one backend
Failure propagationupstream-failed reaches every later stage
Start-up validationcycles, unreachable stages, route targets
Route lineageevery record carries the stages it passed

StageWeaver is the framework that turns single-stage workers into a graph. A graph is a list of stage declarations: each stage names its upstream stages, a policy for waiting on them, and optionally a routing function. Stage authors never see the graph.

It supports arbitrary DAGs: straight chains, fan-out where one stage feeds many, and per-sample routing, where a routing function inspects what a stage produced and returns the stages to send each sample to.

Fan-in with two policies: a stage can wait for all of its inputs, or start on any one of them. And several independent roots and several sinks, each a stage.

Stages can share one model backend: stages in the same initialization group sit under one group-leader process that owns the backend. And failure propagation: if a stage fails a sample, every later stage marks it upstream-failed when it next looks, so no stage waits forever for an input that will never arrive; resetting a derived upstream-failed is always safe, which makes fix-and-rerun possible.

Validation at start-up: acyclicity, reachability, routing-target isolation and the split between the two activation paths. And every output records the stages its sample passed through, so any record can be traced through the graph. Bit positions are stored in 64-bit integers; a wider bit string would serve any number of stages. Graphs are acyclic.

Interface

What a pipeline author writes

# a root stage with a routing function StageConfig(name="understand", is_root=True, routing_fn=route_by_page_type, ...) # routing target: entered only by routing StageConfig(name="charts", upstream_stages=[], ...) # fan-in stage: starts on any one input StageConfig(name="questions", upstream_stages=["charts","tables","text"], wait_for="any", ...) def route_by_page_type(outputs): return {k: [o["page_type"]] for k, o in outputs.items()}
# a model stage: prompt and validation class PromptAndValidation: def get_image_specific_prompt( self, image, logger, inputs=None): return self.prompt_str, [image] def preprocess_vlm_output(self, raw): return json.loads(raw) def validate_output(self, out): if not out.get("question"): raise ValueError("no question") return True
76 lines of configuration: a three-stage routed graph
113 lines: six stages, three model servers, 32 browser workers
Claiming, batching, retries, commit, recovery and hand-off belong to the engine
The same command starts a stage on every node, and restarts it after any failure.

A graph is a list of stage declarations, and a routing function returns, for each sample, the stages to send it to. The left listing declares the first three stages of the workload graph: a root with a routing function, a routing target with no inputs, and a fan-in stage that starts on any one of three inputs.

A model stage is a prompt and a validator, plus a few arguments naming the database, the backend and the model. Claiming, batching, retries, error classes, commit, recovery and hand-off belong to the engine.

A three-stage routed graph is 76 lines of configuration; a six-stage graph with three model servers and 32 browser workers is 113.

And operationally: the same command starts the stage on every node, and the same command restarts it after anything goes wrong. There is no recovery procedure to run.

Comparison · from each system’s documentation

Existing systems against three needs

yespartlynono durable shared state, or not measured

The table sets thirteen systems against the three needs from the start: dynamic graphs, crash safety, and a shared, changing cluster, plus the cost of making a run durable. These are judged from each system's documentation.

LLM and synthetic-data frameworks, distilabel, SyGra, LangGraph and Matrix, express conditional graphs well, but inside one process, or with at-most-once delivery. Matrix has no master but marks work on a crashed agent failed.

Batch data-processing frameworks, NeMo Curator, Data-Juicer, DataTrove and Ray Data, run mostly linear operator chains under a driver, which the cluster can take away.

Workflow and stream engines, Flink, ExoFlow and Airflow, add routing and exactly-once under a job manager or scheduler.

Durable-execution engines, DBOS and Temporal, come closest: a workflow per sample, content routing, any machine, self-healing. But they make every step of every sample a transaction that stores its output, and they retry a failed call on the sample's own budget, so a server outage becomes a hole in the dataset. The last group of columns is the cost of durability, which we measure for DBOS, Temporal and ours.

None of the thirteen meets all three needs. The next slides are the measured comparison with the two closest systems. Scope of the claim: we compare on the properties in the table; DBOS and Temporal offer timers, signals and side-effecting steps that we do not.

Same PostgreSQL · same emulated servers · 32 KB answers

Against DBOS and Temporal

Throughput at 32 nodes

pages per second

DBOS

Flat from 16 nodes. 84–92 % of backends wait in COMMIT for the standby, ~320 MB/s of log, primary CPU at 15 %.

Temporal

Peaks at 546 on 4 nodes. Four instances of each service give 542: same replication wait.

Grows with every node. Primary uses 9 of 192 cores. Replication waits in 8 % of samples.

Emulated model servers; each configuration ran once · paper §7.3

The comparison with the two systems that already survive crashes, route per sample and run across machines. We ran the same pipeline on both, each page one durable workflow with one step per stage, on the same PostgreSQL server and the same four emulated servers per node, with each emulated node holding as many requests in flight as ours.

To isolate database load we made the emulated servers answer in 20 milliseconds so inference would not limit throughput, gave every answer 32 kilobytes, about 8,000 tokens and the size production answers reach, ran each system alone on the database, and added nodes until throughput stopped growing.

DBOS gained nothing from nodes past 16: 1,358 pages per second there, 1,354 at 40. 84 to 92 percent of its active backends were waiting inside COMMIT for the synchronous standby, at about 320 megabytes per second of write-ahead log, while the primary used 15 percent of its CPU. The database's replication path is saturated.

Temporal peaked at 546 on 4 nodes and stayed between 260 and 390 from 8 to 32 nodes. Four instances of each of its services gave 542 at 4 nodes, so its limit is the same replication wait.

Ours kept growing with every added node, to 8,571 pages per second at 32 nodes: 6 times DBOS and 28 times Temporal, with the primary using 9 of 192 cores. A driver replaying our statements without model calls reached over 13,000 pages per second, so the database could give more. Remaining waits are on a lock held by the trigger that maintains per-stage counts; we did not separate that from the emulated clients as the cause. Caveats: this is one deployment of each, each configuration ran once, and Temporal ran on a different host from our first test, so we report its behaviour in one deployment, not its ceiling.

Error handling

Blaming the sample or the system

The sample’s fault

Spends the sample’s retry budget. When exhausted: failed, with the reason recorded.

The system’s fault

Never touches the sample’s budget. Rows return to the queue; the worker pauses or the run stops.

ambiguous

Charged to the system. A wrong charge on a sample is permanent; on the system it costs one retry.

fuse

max(2b, 64) consecutive infrastructure failures with no success stop the run.

On a shared cluster most errors are not the sample's fault. A pipeline that charges a dead server's errors to samples will fail good samples at full speed and leave a hole in the dataset. So every error is classified where it happens, by the process that knows, and the classification answers one question: is the sample at fault, or the system?

The classes are: ok; fail, such as broken JSON, which retries on the validation budget with a stricter prompt; reject, where the server refuses this input and the sample fails on first sight with the reason recorded; infra, such as a server down, a timeout, a 5xx or an aborted generation, which retries on the infrastructure budget; blameless infra, such as a paused worker handing work back, which re-queues with no budget spent; and backend gone, such as an authentication failure or the wrong model, which stops the service and resets rows. One subtle case: a server put to sleep mid-generation returns HTTP 200 with finish reason abort and truncated text, which we class as infrastructure rather than saving it as an answer.

When an error is ambiguous it is charged to the system, because the two mistakes do not cost the same. Failing a good sample is permanent; blaming the system costs one retry.

Two backstops catch what liveness checks cannot see. A fuse stops the run, failing nothing, when max of 2b and 64 consecutive requests fail as infrastructure with no success in between. And a request that fails as infrastructure more than five times while other requests succeed is failed as itself. Before this classification existed, a dead backend marched whole datasets into the failed state.

A model server is down for 10 minutes

Outages and bad samples

DBOS

0good pages failed of 49,894

bounded retries; 106 poison pages keep retrying if retries are unbounded

Temporal

bounded retries; 106 poison pages keep retrying if retries are unbounded

0good pages failed

workers pause and hold no rows; 59 records/s during the outage vs 60 before; each poison page fails after 3 attempts

16 nodes, 5 × 10⁴ pages, 106 poison pages · paper §7.3

This is the experiment that separates the two classes of system most clearly. Over 5 times 10 to the 4 pages on 16 nodes, 106 of them poison pages whose every model call returns malformed output, we took one node's four servers down for ten minutes in the middle of the run.

With the bounded retry policies of the engine defaults, DBOS failed 14,056 of the 49,894 good pages, charged to the samples the outage happened to hit.

Temporal failed 45,099 of them. With unbounded retries no good page failed, but then the 106 poison pages retried forever. Neither engine separates the two cases unless the author writes the distinction into every step.

Our workers on that node paused and held no rows, the run committed 59 records per second during the outage against 60 before it, and each poison page failed after three attempts. The outage was charged to the system, the poison pages to themselves. Note the servers in this experiment refuse connections; a sleeping server instead holds each request until the client's timeout, which makes the outcome depend on that setting rather than on the retry policy.

Production runs: 8.5 M, 6.8 M, 4.5 M and 2.4 M jobs. R4 lost 32 of its 196 servers at once and finished with 41 failures in 2.37 M jobs.

We injected every kind of failure the cluster has shown us and compared the committed index afterwards with that of a run without failures. The pipeline of the workload slide ran over 5 times 10 to the 4 pages on 16 emulated nodes for 72 minutes while a script killed a random process with kill -9 every 30 seconds, killed the container of a whole node every 165 seconds, and every 135 seconds put the servers of one node to sleep in the middle of their requests and woke them a minute later. No operator acted.

After all 198 events the index held all 185,010 records exactly once, with no row stranded and no good page failed. Each restarted process took back the rows it had claimed but not committed, a median of 224 and at most 473, and found its shards clean every one of the 1,402 times it checked.

Separately, we deleted the database primary's pod three times with no grace period. A standby was promoted 20 to 22 seconds later each time; every worker lost its connections, retried and continued without restarting, and all 44,389 records were present once. A third test killed every database connection every 1.2 seconds, 136 times, during a 4,000-item run; no record was lost or duplicated.

In production, every example of the 50.8 million example corpus was generated by this engine. Every run finished at least 99.97 percent of its jobs. Run R3 started on 12 nodes and grew to 46 within eight hours, and 48 later, as the registry listed them, with nothing relaunched, and throughput rose from 49 to 168 answers per second. R4 lost 32 of its 196 servers at once and finished with 41 failures in 2.37 million jobs.

Controlled experiments · emulated servers

Overhead and scaling

98.9–99.7%of a bare client’s throughput

98.9–99.7 % at every scale from 1 to 48 nodes, with no trend

0of linear scaling to 48 nodes

3.88 requests/s on one node, 183.6 on 48

0of throughput when 2 of 12 nodes’ servers slept

the share still serving; no sample failed, lost or written twice

The bare client drives the same servers from a prompt file with no database, ledger or shards · paper §7.4, §7.6

What coordination costs. To isolate it we drive the same hosted servers with a bare client that reads prompts from a file and writes answers to local disk, with no database, ledger or shards, and compare it with the engine running the same single answer stage, over ten minutes of steady state.

At every scale from 1 to 48 nodes the engine reached 98.9 to 99.7 percent of the bare client's throughput, with no trend in the gap. That is the measured version of the cost model: the GPUs are not waiting on coordination.

And it scales: throughput grew from 3.88 requests per second on one node to 183.6 on 48, which is 98.6 percent of linear.

Growing and shrinking: we started 8 nodes, 8 more after 15 minutes and stopped 4 of them 15 minutes later. Each added node's servers answered within 7 seconds of the node starting, and throughput followed the node count. We then put the servers of two of the 12 nodes to sleep for ten minutes: they stopped receiving requests within 5 seconds, throughput held at 82 percent of the 12-node rate, the share still serving, and when they woke they were answering again within 14 seconds.

Scope

Scope and limitations

Where Patram-Ingest fits

  • Long model calls: seconds per sample
  • Records are large and can live outside the database
  • Redoing a bounded group of work is acceptable
  • Acyclic graphs routed by content

Prefer DBOS or Temporal when

  • Timers, signals or human approvals are needed
  • Steps have side effects in the world
  • Step-level recovery matters more than throughput

Known limitations

  • One database; one managed PostgreSQL cluster is a dependency
  • Agent trajectories are replayed whole: tools must tolerate a repeated call
  • At 32 KB answers, throughput is limited by a lock in the per-stage counting trigger
  • Controlled experiments emulate model servers; each configuration ran once

Scope, stated plainly.

The design fits when model calls are long, so coordination can be a small fraction of the runtime; when records are large enough that keeping them out of the database matters; when redoing a bounded group of work is acceptable; and when the graph is acyclic and routed by content.

DBOS and Temporal are the better choice when you need timers, signals, human approvals or side-effecting steps with step-level durability. An agent trajectory in our engine is replayed whole after a failure, so its tools must tolerate a repeated call.

Limitations: the engine depends on one database and runs acyclic graphs only. At 32-kilobyte answers its throughput is limited by a lock in the per-stage counting trigger rather than by the database's resources. The controlled experiments emulate the model servers and each configuration ran once, and Temporal ran on a different host from our first test, so we report one deployment, not its ceiling. In the code, one residual hazard remains documented: the response path still uses shared queues.

What durability unlocks

From durable to self-running

An unattended control loop is only as good as its sensor, and only safe if stopping a node loses nothing.
shipped · v1.9.81

See

One query shows every run, node and stall. Read-only.

shipped · v1.9.92

Stop

Take a run off a node without losing a record.

designed3

Start

Launch a run on a named node, remotely.

planned4

Decide

Scheduling, autoscaling and self-healing, unattended.

Already in the enginerestart recovers a nodedead nodes’ rows are reclaimedliveness from progress, not probespipelines follow shared servers

A durable engine is the foundation for running a fleet without a person watching it. We think of the layer above the engine in four steps, and I will be exact about where each stands.

See: one database connection gives a truthful picture of every run, node and stall. It is strictly read-only. This shipped in version 1.9.8. It matters because a control loop is only as good as its sensor: a person can squint at a stale number and know it is stale, a script cannot.

Stop: take a run off a node without losing work. This shipped in 1.9.9. It is a correctness property of the engine, which is why it was built into the engine. Because every write is ordered and idempotent, stopping a node is safe at any instant.

Start: launch a run on a named node, remotely. This is designed and awaiting validation on one node; nothing is built yet.

Decide: scheduling, autoscaling and self-healing, unattended. This is the goal, and it is planned, not built. Every decision we would want is a query from step one plus an action from step two or three: this node is producing nothing, relaunch it; this run is ahead of schedule, give its nodes to the next one. We deliberately automate a decision only after it has been made by hand enough times.

What the engine already does by itself: a restarted node recovers, dead nodes' rows are reclaimed, liveness comes from progress and not from probes, and pipelines follow the registry of shared servers as servers come and go. That is the self-healing and elasticity at the level of one run. The fleet-level loop is what is next.

Evolution · January to October 2026

How the system evolved

Observed problemDecisionPrinciple
Jan–MarSingle-machine script on SQLite; lock contention at multi-node scalePostgreSQL behind one database layerState lives in the database, not in a process
Apr–MayLinear chains only; branches and merges impossibleStageWeaver DAG router: two bitmasks, one completion callOne mechanism for every topology
Apr–JulGIL contention, image copies, batch barrierOwn process, shared memory, continuous batchingMeasure; remove one bottleneck at a time
AugDead backends marked samples failed; a shared lock froze pools; dead nodes went unnoticedinfra ≠ reject classes; private inboxes; counters kept by a triggerCharge errors to the right party; make absence visible
Sep–OctFixed server URLs; busy servers read as deadHosted backend, registry, liveness from metrics, patram:// URIsPipelines own no GPUs

The system was not designed up front, and the record shows each decision as a response to an observed problem. Five stages, with the principle each one left behind.

January to March: a single-machine script on SQLite. When we moved to several nodes on a shared filesystem, SQLite hit lock contention, so in March the database layer became pluggable and the default moved to PostgreSQL, tested at 12 million image paths. The principle: coordination state lives in the database, not in a process.

April to May: StageWeaver started as a hybrid of processes and threads with a database per stage, which supports only linear chains. The DAG router replaced it: a design document in April, an implementation through May, and a rewire to one process per stage. The principle: one mechanism for every topology.

April to July: throughput. The model service moved out of the pipeline process because of the GIL, then shared memory, then continuous batching, plus 29 percent. The principle: measure, and remove one bottleneck at a time, because each exposes the next.

August: we became honest about failure. A dead backend had marched whole datasets into the failed state, so errors were classified by cause. The 1-in-N pool hang led to private inboxes. And nine of 24 nodes dying unnoticed led to per-node counters maintained by a database trigger, so absence is visible. Principle: charge errors to the right party, and make absence observable.

September to October: a shared fleet. Server URLs stopped being typed in, a registry replaced them, liveness came from metrics, and records are read at the server. Principle: pipelines own no GPUs.

Design principles

Guiding principles

1

No fact before it is true

queue write, then told bit; fsync, then done

2

Every write is idempotent

recovery is the normal code run again

3

Processes hold nothing

no master, lease or heartbeat

4

Charge errors to the right party

ambiguous means the system

5

Own no resource; follow it

pipelines follow a registry of servers

6

Make absence observable

per-node counters, liveness from progress

7

No lock across a failure domain

private inboxes, lock-free status

8

State the limits

known gaps are written down, not hidden

The decisions reduce to eight principles. Each one has a failure behind it.

No fact is recorded before it is true. This one rule governs the hand-off, the commit and the shard upload.

Every write is idempotent, so recovery is not a special mode: the restarted process runs the normal code and converges. Recovery code is the least-tested and worst-failing code, so we avoid having any.

Processes hold nothing that matters. No master, no lease, no heartbeat; a node joins by starting and leaves by dying.

Charge errors to the right party. When unsure, charge the system.

Own no resource; follow it. Pipelines follow servers through a registry, which gives scaling, recovery and sharing from one loop.

Make absence observable. A dying node cannot report its own death, so liveness comes from what a node stops doing, and the sensor rides on writes that already happen.

Do not share a lock across a failure domain: private inboxes, and a lock-free status structure so that the process being watched cannot block the watcher.

State the limits. Known gaps, such as the response-path queues, the single database, and the acyclic graphs, are documented rather than hidden.

Summary

Durable coordination, written in bulk, keeps the GPUs busy and loses no record.

Overlapnon-blocking calls, bounded buffers, a producer always ahead
Orderno fact recorded before it is true; idempotent writes
Graphtwo bitmasks per sample; routing is a write, fan-in is a query
Followpipelines follow shared servers; outages are not bad samples

To summarise. Keeping GPUs busy is a host problem: calls must be non-blocking, about a hundred open per node, with a producer that is always a batch ahead, using processes for failure and GIL isolation, threads for waits, and event loops for in-flight calls. Durable execution is possible cheaply if coordination is written in bulk, idempotent and ordered so no fact is recorded before it is true. StageWeaver reduces dynamic DAGs to two bitmasks per sample and two activation paths. And pipelines follow shared servers and never charge an outage to a sample. Durable state is also what makes the next step possible: a fleet that schedules, scales and heals itself. See and Stop have shipped; Start is designed; Decide is the goal. Thank you; questions.

Likely questions. Why not Kafka or Redis? Every extra component is a new way to fail, and the database costs a few tenths of a percent of runtime. What if PostgreSQL dies? Results on disk stay safe because saving comes first; with managed HA PostgreSQL a failover is 20 to 22 seconds and workers reconnect within a 30-second budget; if the database stays down longer the run aborts and nodes reclaim their rows at next start. Why not per-sample fsync? It is slow on a network filesystem, and the commit group g bounds the redo. Does hash routing hurt balance? It can, so it is opt-in. What about step-level durability? Use DBOS or Temporal for that; our bound is the commit group.
